questions.q: What do SMA, EMA, RSI, MACD, and Bollinger Bands all have in common mathematically?
options: They each require a separate external dataset beyond the price series
They are all deterministic transformations or smooths of the same underlying price series
They only work on intraday data, never daily data
They are all bounded strictly between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Every one of these indicators is built entirely from the price series itself — moving averages, differences of moving averages, and rolling z-scores of price — so none of them introduces new, independent information.

questions.q: In the worked example, SMA(20) and EMA(20) had a correlation of 0.998. What does this illustrate?
options: That EMA is a completely different signal from SMA and should always be preferred
That both are low-pass smooths of the same price window and are, for practical purposes, redundant with each other
That the synthetic price data was generated incorrectly
That moving averages cannot be computed in pandas
questions.explain: SMA and EMA are both smoothing functions over a similar recent window of the same price series, so they move almost identically — feeding a model both adds redundancy, not new information.

questions.q: Why can a technical indicator look 'predictive' when evaluated in-sample on the same historical window it was built from?
options: Because the indicator is mechanically derived from that same price history, so some of the apparent correlation is baked into the arithmetic rather than reflecting real forecasting skill
Because in-sample evaluation always uses a completely separate dataset
Because technical indicators are immune to overfitting by design
Because RSI and MACD use different price data than SMA and EMA
questions.explain: An indicator computed from the last N closes necessarily correlates with what those same closes did, since the correlation is built into the formula — this is a mechanical effect, not evidence that the indicator forecasts anything out-of-sample.

questions.q: What practical problem does a feature set with RSI(14), MACD histogram, and Bollinger %B all correlated above 0.75 with each other create for a regression model?
options: The model will refuse to fit entirely
Multicollinearity — the features act as repeated noisy copies of one underlying momentum signal, which inflates coefficient variance and makes fitted weights unstable
It guarantees the model will have perfect out-of-sample accuracy
It eliminates the need for any further feature engineering
questions.explain: When several features are all different rescalings of the same underlying momentum signal, feeding all of them to a model doesn't add independent information — it creates multicollinearity, which destabilizes coefficient estimates.

questions.q: What is 'curve-fitting' in the context of technical indicator parameters like RSI(14) or MACD(12,26,9)?
options: Using the default parameter values without ever checking them
Tuning an indicator's lookback or smoothing parameters to a specific historical window until it appears predictive there, rather than reflecting a real, stable relationship
Plotting the indicator on a price chart
Combining two indicators into a single composite score
questions.explain: Curve-fitting means adjusting parameters like the RSI lookback or MACD's EMA spans until performance looks good on a particular historical window — a fit to noise in that window rather than a relationship that generalizes.
